title: Neuropeptides shape immunity
objective: Explain how CGRP acts on immune cells through RAMP1-containing receptors.

steps.title: A neuropeptide with an immune address
steps.body: **[[CGRP]]** released by neurons acts on immune (and epithelial) cells that carry its receptor, which includes the component **[[RAMP1]]**. Through this axis, neurons can bias immune activity — for example dialing specific responses up or down.

steps.prompt: For neuronal CGRP to act on an immune cell, what must the immune cell have?
options: The CGRP receptor, including the RAMP1 component itself
Its own internal supply of conducted action potentials
A direct synapse made onto the neuron's own cell body
An enzyme that cuts CGRP into its active form first
steps.explanation: Signaling needs a receptor on the target. CGRP acts on cells bearing its RAMP1-containing receptor — no receptor, no response.

variants.setup: Neurons release CGRP near two cell types; only one responds.
options: Only the responder carries the CGRP receptor
Only the responder can fire action potentials
variants.reveal: The target must express the CGRP (RAMP1) receptor to respond.

steps.setup: You block RAMP1 so immune cells can't receive CGRP, during an infection.
options: The CGRP-driven arm of the response is lost, shifting the outcome
Nothing changes at all, since CGRP never affects immunity
The neurons stop firing their action potentials entirely
The antibody genes are deleted from the immune cells
steps.reveal: Removing the receptor cuts the neuron→immune CGRP signal, changing the response — direct evidence the axis is functional. Yang et al. used exactly this logic in the gut (next, B8).

options: Remove the CGRP-driven arm of the response
Stop the neurons from firing altogether
Delete the antibody genes from the cells
variants.explanation: No receptor means the CGRP signal can't land, changing the outcome.

sources.note: Nociceptors direct goblet cells via a CGRP-RAMP1 axis.
